EdgeCase covers a broad range of graph analysis, but it is rarely the only library in a project.
The data may arrive as a NumPy matrix or a pandas data frame, a colleague's code may build NetworkX
graphs, and a particular algorithm may exist only in igraph. EdgeCase converts graphs to and from
the objects of these libraries directly in memory, without a file in between, so each library can
be used for what it does best.

| Library | To EdgeCase | From EdgeCase | Object |
|---|---|---|---|
| NetworkX | [`from_networkx()`](../reference/from_networkx.qmd) | [`to_networkx()`](../reference/to_networkx.qmd) | `Graph`, `DiGraph`, `MultiGraph`, `MultiDiGraph` |
| igraph | [`from_igraph()`](../reference/from_igraph.qmd) | [`to_igraph()`](../reference/to_igraph.qmd) | `igraph.Graph` |
| NumPy | [`from_numpy_array()`](../reference/from_numpy_array.qmd) | [`to_numpy_array()`](../reference/to_numpy_array.qmd) | a dense adjacency matrix |
| SciPy | [`from_scipy_sparse_array()`](../reference/from_scipy_sparse_array.qmd) | [`to_scipy_sparse_array()`](../reference/to_scipy_sparse_array.qmd) | a sparse adjacency matrix |
| pandas | [`from_pandas_edgelist()`](../reference/from_pandas_edgelist.qmd), [`from_pandas_adjacency()`](../reference/from_pandas_adjacency.qmd) | [`to_pandas_edgelist()`](../reference/to_pandas_edgelist.qmd), [`to_pandas_adjacency()`](../reference/to_pandas_adjacency.qmd) | an edge list or an adjacency data frame |
| two-mode data | [`from_biadjacency_matrix()`](../reference/from_biadjacency_matrix.qmd) | [`biadjacency_matrix()`](../reference/Graph.biadjacency_matrix.qmd) | a rows-by-columns matrix |

These libraries are optional dependencies, imported only when a conversion needs them (see
[Installation](installation.qmd)). The conversions follow the conventions of NetworkX wherever
there is one, so code written for NetworkX's functions of the same names carries over.

## NetworkX

[NetworkX](https://networkx.org) is the most widely used graph library in Python, and a great deal
of existing code, teaching material, and research software is written for it.
[`to_networkx()`](../reference/to_networkx.qmd) converts an EdgeCase graph to a NetworkX graph:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import networkx as nx
import polars as pl

lab = ec.Graph(weighted=True)
lab.add_node("Ada", type="faculty", since=2009)
lab.add_node("Bo", type="postdoc", since=2021)
lab.add_node("Cleo", type="student", since=2022)
lab.add_edge("Ada", "Bo", weight=5.0, rel="coauthor")
lab.add_edge("Ada", "Cleo", weight=2.0, rel="coauthor")
lab.add_edge("Bo", "Cleo", weight=1.0, rel="code")

G = ec.to_networkx(lab)
type(G).__name__, G.nodes["Ada"], G.edges["Ada", "Bo"]
```

The node labels become the NetworkX nodes, so nodes are addressed by name, as is usual in NetworkX
code. The node attributes, including the node `type`, become the node data, and the edge weight
and attributes, including `rel`, become the edge data. A node without a label is represented by
its integer ID. A directed graph becomes a `DiGraph`.

NetworkX's `Graph` and `DiGraph` hold at most one edge between two nodes. When an EdgeCase graph
has parallel edges, `to_networkx()` warns and keeps only the last of them, and
`multigraph=True` gives a `MultiGraph` or `MultiDiGraph` that keeps them all, with the EdgeCase edge
IDs as the edge keys:

```{python}
deliveries = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_edges(
    [("Farm", "Mill"), ("Farm", "Mill"), ("Mill", "Bakery")], auto_create_nodes=True
)
M = ec.to_networkx(deliveries, multigraph=True)
type(M).__name__, M.number_of_edges()
```

[`from_networkx()`](../reference/from_networkx.qmd) converts the other way, for any of the four
NetworkX graph classes. NetworkX's own copy of the karate club, for example, records each member's
eventual club in a `club` attribute and the strength of each friendship as a `weight`:

```{python}
from_nx = ec.from_networkx(nx.karate_club_graph())
from_nx.is_weighted(), from_nx.get_node_df().head(3)
```

The graph is weighted, since the edges have a `weight`; `weighted=` overrides the detection. The
NetworkX nodes, the integers 0 to 33, become the labels, as strings, since EdgeCase labels are
always text. A round trip of a graph with integer nodes therefore gives back a NetworkX graph with
the string nodes `"0"` to `"33"`, which `nx.relabel_nodes(G, int)` turns back into integers.

### Checking results against NetworkX

A common use of the conversion is validation: computing a measure in both libraries and comparing
the results, either to check an analysis or to confirm that the two libraries define a measure
the same way. PageRank on the karate club:

```{python}
karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.pagerank()

nx_scores = nx.pagerank(ec.to_networkx(karate))
ours = dict(karate.get_node_df().select("label", "pagerank").iter_rows())
max(abs(nx_scores[label] - score) for label, score in ours.items())
```

The scores agree to within a few millionths, the tolerance of the two iterative solvers. Many of
EdgeCase's methods are named after their NetworkX counterparts and document where their results or
conventions differ, which makes this kind of comparison straightforward.

## igraph

[igraph](https://python.igraph.org) is a fast graph library with a C core, popular in network
science and especially strong in community detection. [`to_igraph()`](../reference/to_igraph.qmd)
converts a graph to an `igraph.Graph`. igraph numbers its vertices from 0, so the node labels are
kept in the standard `name` vertex attribute, by which igraph can also look vertices up:

```{python}
import igraph as ig

I = ec.to_igraph(lab)
I.vs["name"], I.es[I.get_eid("Ada", "Bo")].attributes()
```

The vertex and edge attributes come along, with the edge weights in the `weight` edge attribute,
which igraph's algorithms use by default. Each edge also gets an `edgecase_edge_id` attribute
holding its EdgeCase edge ID, which links the igraph edges back to the original ones.
[`from_igraph()`](../reference/from_igraph.qmd) converts back, labelling the nodes with their
`name` attribute, or with their vertex indices when there is none.

### Borrowing an algorithm

The conversions make it easy to use an algorithm that EdgeCase doesn't have, and to bring its
result back for further work. igraph implements the Infomap community detection method, which finds
communities by compressing the description of a random walk on the graph. It is randomized, so the
seed of Python's random number generator, which igraph uses, is fixed first:

```{python}
import random

random.seed(1)
I = ec.to_igraph(karate)
infomap = I.community_infomap()
len(infomap), round(infomap.modularity, 3)
```

Infomap finds three communities with a modularity of 0.402. The membership list is in igraph's
vertex order, so it is paired with the vertex names and stored on the EdgeCase graph by label with
[`set_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attrs.qmd):

```{python}
membership = dict(zip(I.vs["name"], infomap.membership))
karate.set_node_attrs("infomap", membership)
karate.plot(color_by="infomap", label_by="label", seed=1)
```

Two of the communities follow the two camps of the club, and the third is a group of five members,
`"4"`, `"5"`, `"6"`, `"10"`, and `"16"`, who are attached to the club mostly through the
instructor. From here, the communities are an ordinary node attribute, available to `plot()`, to
[`modularity()`](../reference/Graph.modularity.qmd), and to every other method that takes a node
attribute. Pairing results with node names rather than relying on positions is the safe pattern
for any conversion, since the libraries need not list the nodes in the same order.

The same route works in the other direction: igraph's `compare_communities()` measures how well
two partitions agree, for example with the normalized mutual information, which compares a
detected partition with the factions the club actually split into:

```{python}
karate.cmty_louvain()
nodes = karate.get_node_df()
{
    method: round(
        ig.compare_communities(nodes["faction"].to_list(), nodes[method].to_list(), method="nmi"), 3
    )
    for method in ["infomap", "cmty_louvain"]
}
```

Infomap's three communities match the two factions somewhat more closely than Louvain's four, as
measured by the normalized mutual information, which is 1 for identical partitions and 0 for
unrelated ones.

## NumPy and SciPy matrices

An adjacency matrix holds a graph as numbers: entry `[i, j]` is the weight of the edge from the
`i`-th node to the `j`-th, and 0 where there is none. In this form, a graph can be handed to the
whole of numerical Python, from linear algebra to machine learning. [Matrices and
spectra](spectral.qmd) describes the matrices that EdgeCase computes itself, such as the
Laplacian; this section covers the conversions.

### Dense arrays

[`to_numpy_array()`](../reference/to_numpy_array.qmd) gives the adjacency matrix as a NumPy array,
with the rows and columns in node ID order. For the marriage network of the Florentine families:

```{python}
import numpy as np

florentine = ec.florentine_families()
A = ec.to_numpy_array(florentine)
A.shape, A.sum()
```

The 15 families and 20 marriages give a 15 × 15 matrix with 40 ones, since an undirected graph
gives a symmetric matrix with each edge in two entries. Matrix products then answer questions about
the graph. The entries of `A @ A` count the walks of two steps, so off the diagonal they count the
neighbors that two families have in common:

```{python}
labels = florentine.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()
common = np.triu(A @ A, k=1)
[(labels[i], labels[j]) for i, j in np.argwhere(common == common.max())]
```

`np.triu(..., k=1)` keeps the entries above the diagonal, so each pair of families is counted
once. No two families share more than two in-laws, and four pairs share two. The labels are listed
in node ID order, the same order as the rows of the matrix, so a row index can be turned straight
into a family name. The rows and columns can be put in another order, or
limited to some of the nodes, with `nodelist=`, which takes node IDs or labels. Other options choose
whether the entries are weights or edge counts (`weighted=`), how parallel edges combine
(`multigraph_weight=`, which sums them by default), and the value for pairs with no edge
(`nonedge=`), such as `float("inf")` for a matrix of distances.

### Sparse matrices

A dense matrix has an entry for every pair of nodes, so it grows with the square of the number of
nodes: a graph of 100,000 nodes would need 80 GB. Real networks are sparse, with far fewer edges
than pairs, and [`to_scipy_sparse_array()`](../reference/to_scipy_sparse_array.qmd) stores only the
nonzero entries, in a SciPy sparse array. The western United States power grid, with its 4,941
substations:

```{python}
from scipy.sparse import csgraph
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh

grid = ec.power_grid()
S = ec.to_scipy_sparse_array(grid)
S.shape, S.nnz
```

The matrix stores 13,188 entries, two for each of the 6,594 lines, instead of the 24 million of a
dense matrix. The CSR format is the default and suits arithmetic and linear algebra, and `format=`
chooses another, such as `"coo"` or `"csc"`. SciPy's sparse graph routines and solvers then work on
the matrix directly, such as `csgraph.connected_components()` for the components and `eigsh()` for
the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix:

```{python}
n_components, _ = csgraph.connected_components(S, directed=False)
largest = eigsh(S, k=1, which="LA")[0][0]
n_components, round(largest, 3)
```

The grid is connected, and its largest adjacency eigenvalue is about 7.5. That eigenvalue matters
for spreading processes: its reciprocal approximates the epidemic threshold, the infection rate
above which an outbreak can take hold on the network (see [Spreading and
robustness](spreading.qmd)).

### Graphs from matrices

[`from_numpy_array()`](../reference/from_numpy_array.qmd) and
[`from_scipy_sparse_array()`](../reference/from_scipy_sparse_array.qmd) build a graph from a
matrix: each nonzero entry becomes an edge, weighted by the entry. This is the usual way to turn a
matrix of similarities or correlations into a network. Consider the daily returns of eleven stocks
in three sectors, simulated here with a market-wide movement and a movement of each sector:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
sectors = {
    "tech": ["AAPL", "MSFT", "NVDA", "GOOG"],
    "energy": ["XOM", "CVX", "COP"],
    "banks": ["JPM", "BAC", "WFC", "C"],
}
market = rng.normal(size=250)
returns, tickers = [], []
for stocks in sectors.values():
    sector = rng.normal(size=250)
    for ticker in stocks:
        returns.append(0.3 * market + 0.8 * sector + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=250))
        tickers.append(ticker)

corr = np.corrcoef(returns)
np.round(corr[:5, :5], 2)
```

The tech stocks are strongly correlated with each other and only weakly with Exxon (`XOM`), the
fifth stock. A *correlation network* links the pairs whose correlation is strong. Keeping the
correlations above 0.6 as edge weights, with the diagonal cleared so that no stock is linked to
itself:

```{python}
corr = (corr + corr.T) / 2
adjacency = np.where(np.abs(corr) > 0.6, corr, 0.0)
np.fill_diagonal(adjacency, 0.0)

market_graph = ec.from_numpy_array(adjacency, node_labels=tickers)
market_graph.count_nodes(), market_graph.count_edges(), market_graph.is_weighted()
```

An undirected graph needs a symmetric matrix, and EdgeCase checks this exactly. The first line
makes the matrix exactly symmetric, since floating-point rounding in `corrcoef()` can leave the two
halves different in the last digit; an asymmetric matrix raises an error, unless `directed=True`
says that it describes a directed graph. Each edge is then read once, from the upper triangle.
`node_labels=` names the nodes in row order, and without it they are labelled `"0"`, `"1"`, and so
on. The graph is weighted because some entries aren't 1, and `weighted=` overrides this.

The eleven stocks are linked by 15 strong correlations, and community detection recovers the
sectors:

```{python}
market_graph.cmty_louvain()
market_graph.get_node_df().group_by("cmty_louvain").agg(pl.col("label")).sort("cmty_louvain")
```

`nonedge=` sets the value that means "no edge", for matrices that use something other than 0,
such as `float("inf")` in a distance matrix. With `parallel_edges=True`, each entry is a count of
parallel edges, so an entry of 3 gives three edges, which reads back the matrix of an unweighted
multigraph. `from_scipy_sparse_array()` takes the same arguments, and reads only the stored entries,
so a graph of millions of edges can be built from a sparse matrix without ever forming a dense one.

## pandas

[pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org) data frames are the common currency of data analysis in Python.
[`to_pandas_edgelist()`](../reference/to_pandas_edgelist.qmd) gives one row per edge, with the
endpoint labels in `source` and `target` columns, the weight, and the edge attributes:

```{python}
ec.to_pandas_edgelist(lab)
```

[`from_pandas_edgelist()`](../reference/from_pandas_edgelist.qmd) builds a graph from such a table,
whether it comes from pandas or from Polars. `source=` and `target=` name the endpoint columns, and
`edge_attr=` chooses which other columns become edge attributes: none by default, as in NetworkX,
`True` for all of them, or a name or a list of names. A numeric `weight` column sets the weights:

```{python}
trades = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "exporter": ["Chile", "Chile", "Peru", "Brazil"],
        "importer": ["China", "Japan", "China", "China"],
        "weight": [21.4, 3.1, 18.2, 104.3],
        "product": ["copper", "copper", "copper", "soybeans"],
    }
)
exports = ec.from_pandas_edgelist(
    trades, source="exporter", target="importer", edge_attr=True, directed=True
)
exports.get_edge_df()
```

Since EdgeCase works with Polars natively, the `Graph` constructor with `edges_df=` is the more
direct route for Polars tables (see [Building graphs](building-graphs.qmd)), while
`from_pandas_edgelist()` is the drop-in replacement for NetworkX's function of the same name.

[`to_pandas_adjacency()`](../reference/to_pandas_adjacency.qmd) gives the adjacency matrix as a
data frame indexed by the node labels, which is easier to read than a bare array, and
[`from_pandas_adjacency()`](../reference/from_pandas_adjacency.qmd) reads one back:

```{python}
ec.to_pandas_adjacency(lab)
```

## Two-mode data

Two-mode, or bipartite, data usually arrives as a rectangular table rather than as a graph: people
by the events they attended, documents by the words they contain, customers by the products they
bought. [`from_biadjacency_matrix()`](../reference/from_biadjacency_matrix.qmd) turns such a table
into a bipartite graph, with one node per row, one node per column, and an edge for each nonzero
entry:

```{python}
purchases = np.array(
    [
        [1, 0, 2, 0],
        [0, 1, 1, 0],
        [3, 0, 0, 1],
    ]
)
shop = ec.from_biadjacency_matrix(
    purchases,
    row_labels=["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"],
    column_labels=["tea", "coffee", "milk", "honey"],
)
shop.get_node_df()
```

The rows come first and the columns after, and the `bipartite` attribute marks the two sides with 0
and 1, as in NetworkX, which is what [`layout_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bipartite.qmd)
and the projections of [Transforming graphs](transforming.qmd) work with. The counts of the
purchases become edge weights. The matrix need not be square, and it can be a list of rows, a NumPy
array, or a SciPy sparse matrix.

[`biadjacency_matrix()`](../reference/Graph.biadjacency_matrix.qmd) goes the other way. It returns
the matrix with the node IDs of its rows and of its columns, which for the Southern Women network
gives the classic table of the eighteen women and the fourteen events they attended:

```{python}
davis = ec.davis_southern_women()
matrix, rows, columns = davis.biadjacency_matrix()
len(rows), len(columns), sum(map(sum, matrix))
```

The 89 ones of the table are the 89 attendances. `row_nodes=` and `column_nodes=` choose the two
sides and their order, which is needed when a bipartite graph has several components.

## Summary

| Task | Function |
|---|---|
| Use NetworkX code or algorithms | `to_networkx()`, `from_networkx()` |
| Keep parallel edges in NetworkX | `to_networkx(multigraph=True)` |
| Use igraph algorithms | `to_igraph()`, `from_igraph()` |
| Do linear algebra on the adjacency matrix | `to_numpy_array()`, `to_scipy_sparse_array()` |
| Build a graph from a similarity or correlation matrix | `from_numpy_array()`, `from_scipy_sparse_array()` |
| Exchange edge lists with pandas code | `to_pandas_edgelist()`, `from_pandas_edgelist()` |
| Read an adjacency table | `from_pandas_adjacency()` |
| Build a bipartite graph from a rows-by-columns table | `from_biadjacency_matrix()` |
| Get the rows-by-columns table of a bipartite graph | `biadjacency_matrix()` |

Whichever library computes a result, the pattern for bringing it back is the same: pair each value
with its node label, and store it with `set_node_attrs()`, so the result joins the rest of the
graph's data.
